_meta.baseline_commit: signalvsnoise-v8 (owner-supplied researched rebuild: web-search pre-pass + cited synthesis)
_meta.v5_note: v4's regex (CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE) was verb-conjugation-specific ('evidence shows/suggests/supports') and missed 12 of 13 real violations in the very next live test, a parenting/screen-time topic: 'the evidence tends to show,' 'observational research,' 'reviews of homework research... broadly recognized in ... literature,' 'researchers argue,' 'is associated with,' 'historically,' 'documented,' 'the evidence on X is Y.' Narrow verb-matching does not generalize across the many ways a model phrases 'I reviewed a body of evidence' — v5's list is now broad WORD/PHRASE matching (evidence/research + up to 3 words + a wide verb set, bare 'literature'/'historically'/'documented'/'associated with', etc.), verified against all 13 new violations plus 7 legitimate ALLOWED sentences (0 false positives, 0 false negatives) before shipping. ARCHITECTURE CHANGE: enforcement moved from a whole-CALL regenerate (v4) to PER-FIELD regenerate (v5) — enforceClaimModeFields()/regenerateField()/setAtPath() rewrite only the flagged sentence (cheap, MODELS.FAST, no JSON schema to fill), preserving everything the model got right instead of risking a whole-half regenerate trading one violation for a different one elsewhere. A field that still fails after its one regeneration attempt is left as-is and the EXISTING structural clean()-filter (unchanged) drops the enclosing item, same fallback as before. NEW: a traceability/scope-creep guard (rule 21 extended + 5 new outputGuard entries) — the same live test also introduced 'free-range parenting' and invented 'the core of free-range parenting' as a model-generated definition, neither of which the visitor raised (visitor supplied only screen time, tiger vs. free-range as a *label pair*, and homework — not a definition of any of them). Rule 21 now states an explicit traceability test (A: a supplied claim, B: a necessary distinction, C: an examined source — if none apply, don't write it). Also reinforced: rule 26 (new) — the_signal doesn't need one item per noise item, don't insert an unprompted epistemic lesson (e.g. 'before-and-after comparisons') the visitor didn't raise, don't invent an individual child/person to apply a population claim to (that belongs in what_general_claims_cant_decide, not the general bottom line). UI: a 'CLAIM ANALYSIS' mode badge with a tooltip now renders under ANALYZING (source_analysis/verified_research labels are unreachable today — this tool performs no live retrieval — and are not yet built; add them only if that capability is ever added). Catalog copy (src/data/tools.js description/seoDescription/primer.get) and svn_tagline reworded away from 'stronger evidence'/'genuinely unsettled' framing that implied the tool always has access to an evidence base, per the same principle as SOURCE MODE. Live-tested against the exact parenting/screen-time/homework scenario (0 banned-phrase hits, 0 field-fix regenerations needed — the strengthened prompt got it right without needing the backstop this time; the backstop's correctness was verified separately via 20 unit test cases against the regex directly). DO NOT revert to whole-call regeneration or narrow the banned-phrase list back to verb-conjugation matching — both were the specific gaps this pass closed.
_meta.v4_note: A THIRD 'final corrections' pass, same day as v3, found the identical literature-review-voice failure in a domain not yet tested — finance ('persistent tracking of fund returns... across multiple markets and asset classes,' 'the evidence covers funds that survived long enough to be measured,' a fabricated survivorship-bias limitation for a dataset never examined). Three prompt-only passes had not fully suppressed this, so v4 adds what they didn't have: a deterministic, ENGLISH-ONLY code-level backstop (see signal-vs-noise.js's CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE / findBannedPhrase / callClaimModeChecked) — every prose field is scanned against a fixed phrase list, a violating half is regenerated once with the exact offending phrase quoted back at it, and any array item that still violates after that is silently dropped rather than shown. The prompt still tries hard to get it right the first time (extensive new PERSONALITY rules, worked BAD/GOOD examples for the fee/valuation/real-estate/survivorship/professional-referral/ranking-against-unnamed-alternatives failures) — the regex is the guarantee, not a replacement for it. SCHEMA CHANGE: genuinely_debated (with nullable what_supports_one_view/another_view, introduced in v3) is REMOVED entirely and replaced by two separate top-level arrays: still_worth_verifying[] ({question, why_it_matters, what_would_help} — a genuinely unresolved GENERAL empirical question, never a fabricated two-sided debate) and what_general_claims_cant_decide[] (plain strings — person-specific questions a general analysis can never resolve, e.g. 'whether direct real estate fits your actual situation'). v3's null-views mechanism for person-dependent questions is superseded by this split, not extended. Response also gains analysis_mode ('claim_analysis', hard-locked in code, not model-self-reported) and sources_examined (always [] today — no source-paste feature exists). Caps changed: the_signal 4->3, still_worth_verifying capped at 2 (was genuinely_debated at 3), what_general_claims_cant_decide capped at 3, the_bottom_line.what_would_change_the_answer 2->3. i18n: svn_nuance reworded 'Limits:' -> "What it doesn't establish:"; svn_debated_header reworded 'Still Unsettled' -> 'Still Worth Verifying'; new keys svn_verify_why/svn_verify_would_help/svn_cant_decide_header; svn_one_view/svn_another_view/svn_why_unsettled are now orphaned (left in the locale files, no longer referenced in JSX — the two-sided-debate UI was removed, not relabeled). outputGuard.prohibit grew from 28 to 37 entries. DO NOT reverse the schema split or the code-level regex backstop — three prompt-only passes already proved insufficient on their own.
_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run (npm run check:golden signal-vs-noise). v2 (2026-09-09) fixed the health-domain instances of the tool implying a literature review it never performed. v3 (2026-09-10) fixed the SAME failure mode recurring in a non-health (career/labor) domain — 'wage data shows,' an invented MBA-recruiting market map, an invented causal mechanism for job-switching pay, a strawmanned 'follow your passion' critique, an extra unrequested career-advice claim, two noise_type mislabels, an unsupported publicity/selection-bias claim used to rebut an overclaim with another overclaim, debate-club phrasing, and a STILL UNSETTLED section forced into a two-sided-evidence shape it didn't have for a person-dependent question. v4 (same day) is documented in v4_note above. v5 (2026-09-10) is documented in v5_note above. v6 (2026-09-10) is documented in v6_note above.
_meta.prior_notes: v2 (2026-09-09) was a full owner-supplied rewrite: the v1 tool asserted "real consensus," named specific actors as "generating noise," and invoked specific research designs, biomarkers, genetic variants, and validation findings from memory as though it had performed a sourced evidence review — exactly the authority the tool was never in a position to claim. Schema changed completely from v1 (why_this_field_is_noisy -> framing; the_signal.items[].why_we_know_this -> basis; .the_nuance -> limits; genuinely_debated[].side_a/side_b -> what_supports_one_view/what_supports_another_view (later removed entirely in v4); the_noise[] gained what_the_evidence_supports_instead alongside renamed what_went_wrong (was the_problem); the_bottom_line's three single-string fields became three arrays; sources_of_noise[].actor/incentive/how_to_spot_it -> source_type/how_it_distorts/how_to_recognize_it, no longer naming an accused actor). Guards added that pass: NO_QUOTE_RULE, router.outputStandard='v2' + outputGuard, and a post-guard structural validation pass (see code comment: the guard mutates its argument in place and its repair pass can leave a field incomplete despite instructions not to).
_meta.v6_note: A FOURTH 'final corrections' pass, sleep domain, confirmed the deterministic claim_analysis mode switch (v4) had finally killed the fake-literature-review voice, but found a narrower, different failure: unlabeled empirical premises imported from memory that never use evidence-provenance wording at all, so CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE cannot catch them ('most adults need roughly 7-9 hours', 'light exposure is one input to the body's circadian timing system', 'additional sleep after restriction can reduce sleepiness'), plus a logical non-sequitur reasoning backward from a metaphor's usefulness to a fact about the thing it describes ('if a single recovery night fully erased all sleep debt, the metaphor wouldn't be useful'), plus a bottom line that broke back into sleep/parenting/finance guidance and invented personal context nobody supplied in what_would_change_the_answer. FIX (prompt-level, not regex — this class of error has no stable lexical marker a regex can key on): new rule 27 ('WHAT AUTHORIZES THIS SENTENCE?') gives the model an explicit 3-way test before writing any factual sentence — A. USER_CLAIM (the visitor supplied it), B. LOGIC (follows from the claim's own structure, no empirical finding needed), C. LABELED_BACKGROUND (genuinely ordinary vocabulary-only background, used sparingly, never the central empirical answer) — rewrite or remove if none apply. New rule 28 fixes the metaphor non-sequitur (critique what a metaphor fails to establish, never reason backward from 'what would make it useful'). New rule 29 locks the bottom line to summarizing the claim analysis only, and reserves personal-situation language in what_would_change_the_answer for when the visitor actually supplied enough personal context to identify a real gap. NORTH STAR gained a prepended 3-line frame: use knowledge to understand the claim, logic to test it, evidence to settle it. TRAP HIT AND FIXED DURING THIS PASS: the rule 27/29 illustrative BAD examples quoted the exact attractor phrase 'additional sleep after restriction can reduce sleepiness' TWICE, verbatim — live testing showed the model echoing that near-verbatim phrase straight into output (a known trap: worked BAD-example text gets copied rather than avoided, see deftbrain-voice-prompt-traps memory). Fixed by rewriting both examples to describe the ERROR PATTERN in the abstract (no specific number, no specific mechanism, no specific magnitude-of-benefit claim to copy) plus an explicit 'this is illustrating a pattern, not a script — a close paraphrase is the same violation' instruction. Verified 0 banned-phrase / 0 attractor-phrase hits across 3 consecutive live regenerations of the exact sleep scenario after the reword (the run before the reword produced the attractor phrase; the runs after did not). UI: added a visible 'No outside sources reviewed' sub-label beside the CLAIM ANALYSIS badge (the existing badge only had it in a hover tooltip, poor discoverability) and a 'Research These Claims' disclosure at the end of results, built from still_worth_verifying (falling back to what_would_change_the_answer) with one external search-engine link per open question — pure frontend, no new backend capability. This is deliberately NOT a live-retrieval / verified-research mode: the tool has no wired search or fetch capability, and building real retrieval is an infrastructure decision (external dependency, cost per request, latency, reliability) flagged to the owner rather than silently built or silently dropped, same position as the v5 note. i18n: svn_honest_uncertainty relabeled '? What Could Change the Answer' -> '? What Would Help' across all 13 languages (claim-analysis mode is never about the visitor's personal situation, so the more evidence-focused label is now the default; a personalized 'what could change the answer' framing would need a genuinely supplied personal-context case, which this tool does not yet branch on). New keys: svn_no_sources_reviewed, svn_research_these_claims, svn_research_intro, svn_search_this (13 languages each). DO NOT re-quote a specific number, mechanism, or magnitude figure in rule 27/28/29's illustrative examples — describe the pattern, never the sentence.
_meta.v7_note: V7 replaces 'regex + one regen' with a five-stage CLAIM ANALYSIS VALIDATION PIPELINE in the route: (1) CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE, demoted to cheap first-pass detection; (2) a SEMANTIC EMPIRICAL-RESOLUTION CHECK — a judged call asking ONE narrow question per field (does this text assert or rely on a real-world proposition that was not supplied, not sourced in this run, and materially helps decide the claim? hedges do not convert FAIL to PASS); (3) one per-field REWRITE with the owner's exact rewrite prompt; (4) REVALIDATE the rewrite alone (regex + judge, batch size 1); (5) a fixed, LOCALIZED SAFE FALLBACK per field type (13 languages, in CLAIM_MODE_FALLBACKS) — never a second regeneration, because a validator/regenerator loop is exactly how the model finds new vocabulary for the same assertion. Fields with no fallback (a signal item's claim, a still_worth_verifying question, a sources_of_noise field, a person-specific item) are blanked so the structural filter drops the item. 5b: a signal item whose basis fell back gets its CLAIM re-judged alone and dropped unless it passes — a fixed basis under an unlicensed claim would lend it the very logical veneer the pipeline removes. WHY: five consecutive prompt-only passes (tool rules 14/27-29, then two rounds of the global epistemics contract) all failed the same live nutrition test the same way — the model stopped saying 'research shows' and started stating bare or hedged premises ('hormones regulate appetite and energy expenditure', 'meal timing may interact with circadian rhythms', 'intermittent fasting is a workable structure for some people'), or laundering them through 'this follows from the accounting relationship'. No lexical marker exists for that; a phrase list structurally cannot see it. MEASURED DURING BUILD: (a) judge recall collapses with batch size — one call over all 48 fields flagged 3 and missed the two plainest violations; the same two fields alone were both flagged in 1.7s — hence SEMANTIC_BATCH_SIZE=6, parallel; (b) the judge is consistent (3/3) on what it flags but neighborhood-sensitive, hence two offset passes unioned at stage 2; (c) the judge itself got laundered by 'this follows from the structure...' framing until told to judge every sentence on its own. Standalone replay of a leaked response through the finished pipeline: semantic=9 rewritten=6 fallback=2 blanked=1, and a fresh judge pass over the result found the flagship leaks gone. Live: 4 consecutive runs, fallbacks firing 1-5 times per run, route time ~60s (parallel judge calls; +10-20s vs v6). COST: roughly 20-35 small MODELS.SMART calls per request on a leaky response — a deliberate trade for a tool whose entire promise is this discipline. GOLDEN: schema unchanged; sources_of_noise and what_general_claims_cant_decide are now optionalSections on every case because the pipeline legitimately empties them (their fields have no fallback text, so a flagged item drops). DO NOT: collapse the judge back to one big batch; add a second regeneration attempt; let a rewrite through when its recheck was unavailable; give sources_of_noise/still_worth_verifying fields a fallback (they'd become filler).
_meta.v7_1_note: V7.1 (same day): SEMANTIC_CHECK_SYSTEM is now the owner's supplied validation prompt (PASS only if every substantive claim is visitor-supplied or logical analysis needing no extra real-world premise; FAIL on remembered knowledge, unsupplied examples, 'unestablished then asserted anyway', hedge-disguised claims, conclusions not established by validated material; counterfactual key test), wrapped in the batch/JSON contract plus a CLARIFICATIONS block. Measured: as written it over-flagged the tool's own correct output (flagged 'is an empirical question this analysis cannot settle'; one live run blanked the whole Signal section). Restoring the owner's earlier 'ignore statements that merely define / analyze wording / identify missing info / say evidence is needed' list fixed that (replay: blanked 1 -> 0, signal item kept). Live cost with the final prompt on the nutrition scenario: 12 fallbacks in one run (5/8 bottom-line items boilerplate) — the rule applied faithfully; boilerplate density is the owner's call, documented in the tool notes. Flagship BAD sentences ('hormonal factors operate within the energy-balance relationship', 'not competing explanations — they interact') added verbatim to MUST-fail examples after the solo re-judge passed one of them once.
_meta.v7_2_note: V7.2 (same day): fallback PRESENTATION only, judge untouched. (1) bottom_line fallback split into per-list wording takeaway/skeptical/would_help, each with a _many variant, 13 languages. (2) optional sub-fields (kernel_of_truth, signal limits) are OMITTED on failure (null) instead of replaced — UI renders them only when present. (3) collapseBottomLineFallbacks: within each bottom-line list, survivors untouched, all fallback items fold into at most one bullet placed last (singular wording for one failure, _many for several) — a variable-length Bottom Line, per DEFTBRAIN_OUTPUT_STANDARD_V2's preference for omission over redundant completeness. Bug caught by the fallback unit test before shipping: English would_help fallbacks began 'Evidence about…', matching CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE, so the structural filter would have dropped the collapsed bullet; reworded. Live run 7: one collapsed takeaway bullet, kernels 3/4 (one omitted), no repeated fallbacks.
_meta.v8_note: V8 (2026-09-11): owner-supplied rebuild replaces the source-free claim-analysis architecture (V4-V7.2) with research-first: lib/claimResearch.js runs a bounded Anthropic web_search pre-pass through groundedFacts (maxUses default 6 for this tool, 3 everywhere else), returns a structured evidence packet, and the synthesis call (no tools) may make empirical claims ONLY from the packet with source_ids validated in code. New response fields: analysis_mode='verified_research', research_status, researched_at, sources_examined[{id,title,publisher,url,date,source_type}] (pruned to sources actually cited), and source_ids[] on the_signal items / the_noise items / still_worth_verifying items. Cold cache: waits up to SIGNAL_RESEARCH_COLD_WAIT_MS then returns HTTP 503 code:research_unavailable rather than an unresearched answer — so a golden re-run can 503 on a cold server; run the case once to warm (24h TTL), then check. the_noise is now optional (items without a surviving source id drop). The regex/judge/rewrite/fallback machinery and CLAIM_MODE_FALLBACKS are gone; earlier DO-NOT notes in SIGNALVSNOISE-NOTES.md V4-V7.2 are superseded, not reversed. See the V8 section there for kit findings.

input.conflictingAdvice: Index funds always win vs. active management can beat the market, time in market beats timing the market vs. valuations matter, real estate vs. stocks

output.topic_as_understood: Three common investing debates: index funds vs. active management, time in market vs. market timing, and real estate vs. stocks as long-term wealth builders
output.framing: Each of these debates is often posed as a binary when the evidence supports more conditional conclusions — 'usually true for most investors' is not the same as 'always true.' The strongest distortion in all three is collapsing a probabilistic, context-dependent finding into a universal rule.

items.claim: For most retail investors in U.S. large-cap equity, low-cost index funds have a strong track record against the average actively managed fund — especially over long horizons.
items.basis: Over the 15-year period ending 2024, no U.S. equity fund category had a majority of active managers beating their benchmark. In 2025, 79% of active large-cap funds underperformed the S&P 500. The arithmetic explanation — active management is zero-sum before costs, and costs are higher — gives a structural reason to expect this, not just a historical curiosity.
items.limits: Results vary by category; some international and small-cap categories have shown shorter periods of majority active outperformance. The underperformance gap narrows when comparing before-fee returns. A minority of truly active funds with high 'active share' and low fees have shown some ability to add value in certain market conditions.

items.claim: Staying invested in a broad market index over long periods has historically produced positive real returns, and attempting to time the market has a poor track record for typical retail investors.
items.basis: U.S. broad market data from 1936 to 2025 shows no negative returns on any rolling 20-year window, and no negative returns over any rolling period longer than 12 years since 1972. Missing even a small number of the best-performing days — which cluster during high-volatility periods when timers are most likely to be out — substantially reduces long-run returns. Successful timing requires two correct decisions (exit and re-entry), and evidence indicates most investors get one or both wrong.
items.limits: This evidence is U.S.-centric; investors in markets that experienced prolonged or permanent declines would have had different outcomes. The finding applies to broad index participation, not concentrated or illiquid positions. It does not rule out long-horizon, valuation-aware allocation adjustments — only short-term in-and-out timing.

items.claim: Real estate and stocks have produced broadly comparable gross long-run returns globally, but net returns on direct real estate ownership are meaningfully lower once operating costs are properly counted.
items.basis: A large multi-country study covering 1870-2015 found inflation-adjusted total returns of roughly 7% annually for both residential real estate (including rent) and equities (including dividends). However, when maintenance, property taxes, insurance, and management costs are deducted at the property level, net real returns on residential real estate have been estimated at roughly 2.3% — far below the gross figure commonly cited in comparisons with equities.
items.limits: The multi-country averages mask sharp variation by location, time period, and property type. Leverage, rental income, and tax treatment can substantially alter outcomes for individual investors. Direct real estate and REITs behave differently and should not be conflated.

the_noise.claim: Index funds always win over active management
the_noise.noise_label: Always is doing too much work
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: The average actively managed U.S. large-cap fund has underperformed its benchmark over most long-horizon windows studied, and the majority of active funds in most categories fail to beat their benchmarks over 15 years. But 'always' and 'every fund' are not supported.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The strong aggregate evidence against the average active fund gets stretched into a claim that no active fund can outperform under any conditions. The research shows a minority of high-active-share, lower-cost funds in certain market structures have shown evidence of adding value — 'usually loses' is not the same as 'always loses.'
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: The overwhelming odds, especially over long horizons and in large-cap U.S. markets, favor low-cost index funds over the average active alternative. That is a well-supported and practically important conclusion.

the_noise.claim: Valuations do not matter — pure time in market is all that counts
the_noise.noise_label: Conflates short-term timing with long-horizon base rates
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Time in market strongly beats short-term tactical timing for most retail investors. Separately, valuation measures such as the Shiller CAPE have shown meaningful predictive power for long-horizon expected returns — not for when to exit, but for calibrating realistic return expectations.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The 'time in market' evidence, which concerns short-term in-and-out timing decisions, gets overapplied to dismiss any role for valuations in setting return expectations over a decade or more. These are different questions. The CAPE's poor ability to time markets does not negate its demonstrated relationship with 10-to-20-year forward returns.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Trying to use valuations as a short-term market timing signal has not been shown to improve investor outcomes. The anti-timing evidence is real and strong for that specific use case.

still_worth_verifying.question: Does the current CAPE reading of approximately 40.6x (98.8th historical percentile as of September 2026) meaningfully lower expected long-horizon returns, or have structural changes made the historical CAPE baseline obsolete?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: If the historical CAPE-return relationship holds, long-horizon real returns from U.S. equities at current valuations may be substantially below their historical average — relevant to anyone allocating heavily to U.S. stocks today. If structural changes (accounting standards, sector composition, persistently lower real rates) have shifted the baseline upward, the signal is weaker.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Analysis distinguishing how much of the elevated CAPE is explained by structural factors versus speculative premium; out-of-sample tests of CAPE predictive power in post-2002 data; international CAPE comparisons to assess whether U.S. premium is justified.

still_worth_verifying.question: Under what specific conditions — market type, fund characteristics, time horizon — do high-active-share, lower-cost active funds reliably add value net of fees?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: If reliably identifying such funds in advance is possible, the 'just use index funds' conclusion is less universal. If it requires after-the-fact selection, the practical value is limited.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Prospective studies tracking funds identified as high-active-share and low-cost before the measurement period, across multiple market regimes and geographies.

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Whether direct real estate or stocks is better for you depends on your access to capital, ability to manage a property, local market conditions, tax situation, existing diversification, and financing terms — none of which the general evidence can answer.

Whether you should adjust your equity allocation given current CAPE levels depends on your time horizon, liquidity needs, and whether you have a disciplined framework for re-entry — factors the population-level evidence does not resolve for any individual.
Whether a specific active fund is worth its fees depends on its actual active share, cost structure, and the market segment it operates in — not on aggregate SPIVA data.

supported_takeaways: Low-cost broad index funds have beaten the majority of actively managed U.S. large-cap funds over most long horizons studied — the odds strongly favor indexing for a typical investor, even if 'always wins' overstates it.

Staying invested beats short-term market timing for most retail investors; the evidence on missed best-days and re-entry errors is consistent and the long-horizon loss record for U.S. broad indices is essentially zero across periods of 12-20 years.

Real estate and stocks have historically produced similar gross returns globally, but direct real estate ownership carries substantial costs that compress net returns — leverage, tax treatment, and local conditions are the decisive variables, not the asset class label.
treat_skeptically: 'Index funds always win' — the evidence supports 'usually wins on average' and 'the odds heavily favor indexing,' not a universal law.
Gross return comparisons between real estate and stocks that omit operating costs — the net-of-cost gap is large enough to reverse casual conclusions.
Using CAPE or any valuation metric as a short-term timing signal — the evidence supports CAPE as a long-horizon return forecaster, not an exit trigger.
what_would_change_the_answer: Evidence that current elevated CAPE levels are fully explained by structural changes rather than speculative premium would weaken the case for tempering long-horizon U.S. equity return expectations.
Prospective data showing that high-active-share, low-cost active funds can be identified in advance and deliver consistent net-of-fee alpha would qualify the indexing conclusion more substantially.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Average active fund underperformance is real and large, but reporting the average obscures that a minority of funds do outperform. The aggregate statistic gets treated as a statement about every fund, producing 'always' and 'never' claims the data does not support.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Claims that use 'always,' 'never,' or 'impossible' about active management — as opposed to 'most,' 'on average,' or 'the majority.'

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Headline comparisons between asset classes (especially real estate vs. stocks) typically use gross returns. Operating costs for direct real estate are large enough to substantially change the comparison. The conflation makes real estate look more competitive than net evidence supports.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Any real estate return figure that does not specify whether maintenance, taxes, insurance, and management costs have been deducted.

sources_of_noise.source_type: Collapsing different questions into one claim
sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Evidence that short-term market timing is harmful gets used to dismiss the relevance of valuations to long-horizon expected returns — two distinct claims that the evidence treats differently. The simplified framing ('just stay invested, nothing else matters') sounds stronger than the research warrants.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: When 'time in market beats timing' is used to argue that current valuations are irrelevant to expected returns over the next decade — that is a different and less well-supported claim.

input.conflictingAdvice: Indexfonds gewinnen immer vs. aktives Management kann den Markt schlagen, Zeit im Markt schlaegt Markt-Timing vs. Bewertungen sind wichtig

output.topic_as_understood: Drei verbreitete Investmentthesen im Vergleich: Indexfonds vs. aktives Management, langfristiges Halten vs. Markt-Timing, und ob Bewertungskennzahlen (insbesondere CAPE) als Renditeprädiktor nützlich sind.
output.framing: Der entscheidende Unterschied liegt im Zeithorizont und der Formulierung: Aussagen, die über lange Zeiträume statistisch gut belegt sind, werden im Alltag oft als absolute oder universelle Regeln wiedergegeben. Damit überschreiten sie, was die Belege tragen.

items.claim: Über lange Zeiträume underperformen die meisten aktiv gemanagten Aktienfonds ihren Vergleichsindex – und die Outperformance der wenigen Ausnahmen lässt sich kaum zuverlässig im Voraus identifizieren.
items.basis: SPIVA-Daten zeigen, dass über 15 Jahre in keiner einzigen der 22 untersuchten US-Aktienfondskategorien eine Mehrheit der aktiven Manager ihren Benchmark schlug. Die Persistenz-Scorecard ergänzt dies: Fonds, die kurzfristig outperformen, wiederholen das statistisch kaum – bei Large-Cap-Fonds sogar unterhalb einer reinen Zufallsverteilung.
items.limits: Die Daten beziehen sich hauptsächlich auf den US-Markt. Europäische und deutsche Fondslandschaften, andere Anlageklassen sowie bestimmte Nischensegmente können abweichen. Außerdem schwanken die Jahresergebnisse: In der ersten Jahreshälfte 2025 underperformten nur 54 % der Large-Cap-Fonds, deutlich weniger als der langfristige Schnitt.

items.claim: Für die meisten Anleger ist dauerhaftes Investieren dem Versuch überlegen, den richtigen Ein- und Ausstiegszeitpunkt zu treffen.
items.basis: Akademische Studien finden bei aktiv gemanagten Fonds keine belastbaren Belege für Markt-Timing-Fähigkeiten. Morningstar-Daten zeigen, dass Anleger über zehn Jahre rund 1,1 Prozentpunkte pro Jahr weniger als die tatsächliche Fondsrendite erzielten – ein Hinweis auf verhaltensbedingte Timing-Verluste. Wer die stärksten Handelstage verpasst, verliert überproportional, weil diese oft direkt auf starke Kursrückgänge folgen.
items.limits: Die Analyse der 'verpassten besten Tage' ist methodisch angreifbar: Wer auch die schlechtesten Tage meidet, könnte besser abschneiden – doch diese ex ante zu identifizieren gilt als kaum möglich. Regelbasierte Trendfolge-Ansätze sind konzeptuell von spontanem Timing zu unterscheiden und durch den Befund nicht ausgeschlossen.

items.claim: Das Shiller-CAPE hat eine dokumentierte, statistisch negative Beziehung zu nachfolgenden 10-Jahres-Aktienrenditen – hohe Bewertungen gehen tendenziell mit niedrigeren langfristigen Renditen einher.
items.basis: Forschungen zeigen diese Beziehung für 17 MSCI-Länderindizes seit 1979. Das Maß wird von Zentralbanken, IWF und BIZ als Referenzgröße genutzt. Eine aktuellere Studie (Juni 2026) weist zudem darauf hin, dass eine kapitalgewichtete CAPE-Variante die Prognosekraft verbessert.
items.limits: Die Vorhersagekraft gilt vorwiegend für 10-Jahres-Horizonte; für kürzere Zeiträume ist sie deutlich schwächer. Methodische Kritikpunkte (veränderte Bilanzregeln, Indexzusammensetzung) schränken historische Vergleiche ein. Hohe Bewertungen schließen jahrelange weitere Kursanstiege nicht aus.

the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Über lange Zeiträume (10-15 Jahre) underperformt eine große Mehrheit aktiver Fonds ihren Index. In einzelnen Jahren oder Marktsegmenten kann aktives Management kurzfristig besser abschneiden.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Das Wort 'immer' behauptet eine absolute Ausnahmslosigkeit, die die Daten nicht stützen. SPIVA zeigt jährliche Schwankungen (z. B. 54 % Underperformance im ersten Halbjahr 2025 statt der langfristigen ~64-79 %). 'Immer' gilt weder für jeden Zeitraum noch für jedes Marktsegment.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Die Datenlage spricht langfristig und über die meisten Kategorien klar für Indexfonds – besonders wenn man Fonds berücksichtigt, die in der Zwischenzeit fusioniert oder liquidiert wurden.

the_noise.claim: Bewertungen sind wichtig – implizit als kurzfristiger Handlungsauslöser.
the_noise.noise_label: Langfristiger Prädiktor wird als Timing-Signal missverstanden
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: CAPE ist ein statistisch belegter Prädiktor für 10-Jahres-Renditen, nicht für kurzfristige Marktbewegungen. Als Basis für taktisches Timing – z. B. US-Aktien bei hohem CAPE untergewichten – hat es historisch nicht zuverlässig besser abgeschnitten als einfaches Buy-and-Hold.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Die Formulierung 'Bewertungen sind wichtig' impliziert oft, dass man bei hohen Bewertungen jetzt handeln sollte. Die Belege stützen aber nur einen langfristigen statistischen Zusammenhang, keinen verlässlichen kurzfristigen Handlungsauslöser.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Für einen Anleger mit sehr langem Horizont (10+ Jahre) liefert CAPE eine nützliche Einschätzung der Ertragschancen verschiedener Märkte – als grober Kompass, nicht als Präzisionsinstrument.

still_worth_verifying.question: Wie gut funktionieren Indexfonds-Argumente speziell für den deutschen und europäischen Markt?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: SPIVA-Daten stammen überwiegend aus dem US-Markt. Fondskosten, Regulierung und Marktstruktur in Deutschland und Europa können die Ergebnisse verschieben.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Europäische SPIVA-Scorecards oder vergleichbare Studien für in Deutschland vertriebene Fonds würden helfen, die These auf den hiesigen Markt zu übertragen.

still_worth_verifying.question: Verbessert eine kapitalgewichtete CAPE-Variante die Renditeprognosekraft gegenüber dem klassischen Shiller-CAPE tatsächlich belastbar?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Wenn ja, könnte das die praktische Nutzbarkeit von Bewertungskennzahlen für die langfristige Asset-Allocation stärken.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Unabhängige Replikation der Juni-2026-Studie über verschiedene Marktphasen und Länder hinweg.

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Ob Indexfonds für den individuellen Anleger die passende Wahl sind, hängt von Zeithorizont, Risikobereitschaft, Steuersituation und verfügbaren Produkten ab – das entscheidet keine allgemeine Statistik.
Ob und wie stark CAPE-basierte Überlegungen die persönliche Asset-Allocation beeinflussen sollten, hängt davon ab, wie viele Jahre der Anleger tatsächlich investiert bleiben kann und will.
Ob regelbasierte Trendfolge-Ansätze für eine bestimmte Person Sinn ergeben, lässt sich aus den vorliegenden Belegen nicht ableiten.

supported_takeaways: Über lange Zeiträume underperformt eine klare Mehrheit aktiv gemanagter Aktienfonds ihren Index, und die Ausnahmen lassen sich kaum im Voraus identifizieren – das stützt Indexfonds als Ausgangspunkt, ohne 'immer' zu rechtfertigen.
Dauerhaft investiert bleiben schlägt für die meisten Anleger den Versuch, den Markt zu timen – verhaltensbedingte Verluste durch schlechtes Timing sind empirisch dokumentiert.
CAPE ist ein nützlicher grober Kompass für langfristige Renditeerwartungen verschiedener Märkte, aber kein zuverlässiges Signal für kurzfristige Handlungen.
treat_skeptically: 'Indexfonds gewinnen immer' – das Wort 'immer' überschreitet, was die Daten belegen.
Hohe CAPE-Werte als unmittelbaren Handlungsauslöser zu nutzen – die Belege stützen keinen verlässlichen kurzfristigen Timing-Vorteil daraus.
what_would_change_the_answer: Belastbare europäische bzw. deutsche Fondsdaten könnten die Indexfonds-Argumentation für hiesige Anleger stärken oder abschwächen.
Unabhängige Replikation der kapitalgewichteten CAPE-Variante könnte die praktische Nutzbarkeit von Bewertungskennzahlen für die Asset-Allocation neu bewerten.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Aus 'in den meisten Fällen über lange Zeiträume' wird 'immer' oder 'nie' – weil absolute Aussagen leichter zu kommunizieren und zu merken sind als statistisch kalibrierte.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Immer, nie, immer besser, schlägt grundsätzlich – Quantoren ohne Einschränkung zu Zeitraum oder Marktsegment.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Befunde, die für 10-Jahres-Horizonte gelten (z. B. CAPE-Prognosekraft), werden auf kürzere Zeiträume übertragen, für die die Belege deutlich schwächer sind.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Wenn eine Empfehlung nicht angibt, für welchen Zeithorizont sie gilt, ist das ein Warnsignal.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Vergleiche, die nur noch existierende Fonds berücksichtigen, überschätzen die Erfolgsquote aktiver Manager, weil schlechte Fonds geschlossen oder fusioniert werden.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Studien oder Werbeaussagen, die keine Angabe machen, ob liquidierte oder fusionierte Fonds einbezogen wurden.

input.conflictingAdvice: Screen time is destroying kids vs. it depends on content, tiger parenting vs. free-range, homework helps vs. homework is harmful

output.topic_as_understood: Four contested parenting claims: whether screen time universally harms children, whether tiger parenting outperforms other styles, whether free-range parenting produces better outcomes than overprotective parenting, and whether homework helps or hurts academic achievement.
output.framing: Most of these conflicts are not about which side is simply right — they are about universalized claims being applied to outcomes that depend heavily on dose, content, age, and context. The evidence mostly supports narrower, conditional versions of each claim.

items.claim: Screen time type and content matter, not just total hours — passive TV-style use is more consistently linked to worse outcomes than educational or interactive use.
items.basis: A longitudinal study of over 4,000 Australian children found that passive screen time was linked to worse outcomes, while educational screen time showed positive educational associations and no significant negative associations with other outcomes. A 2026 systematic review found that passive use was linked to reduced attention in preschoolers, while interactive and educational use tended to show more favorable attentional outcomes. Both sources agree the field has been held back by treating all screen time as a single measure.
items.limits: Even the content distinctions are imprecise: 'interactive' covers qualitatively different activities, and educational quality varies by specific app or platform. All identified effects in the Australian study were small (standardized effects under 0.07). Evidence is largely correlational.

items.claim: Supportive parenting — high warmth combined with high structure — is associated with better child outcomes than high-pressure, low-warmth tiger parenting.
items.basis: An eight-year longitudinal study of over 400 Asian-American families found supportive parenting was the most common style and was linked to the best developmental outcomes and highest GPA. Tiger parenting in that study was associated with higher rates of depressive symptoms, academic pressure, and feelings of alienation. A study of Hong Kong children also found that child-perceived tiger parenting was positively associated with child anxiety.
items.limits: Research is concentrated in Asian and Asian-American samples; how well findings transfer to other cultural contexts is unclear. Tiger parenting combines high demandingness with high involvement, making it hard to isolate which aspect drives which outcome.

items.claim: The homework-achievement relationship is real for older students but weak to absent for younger ones.
items.basis: A widely cited meta-analysis found a positive correlation between homework and achievement that was stronger for grades 7-12 and weak for younger students. A 2017 meta-analysis found the effect size grows substantially through upper elementary and high school, while the impact for grades 1-4 is limited.
items.limits: Most homework research is correlational, not experimental. Cooper's earlier foundational review concluded there is no evidence that homework improves performance for elementary students. Excessive homework is also linked to fatigue and negative attitudes toward learning. A meta-analysis using PISA data found parental help with homework was associated with lower achievement, suggesting involvement effects can be counterproductive.

the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Excessive screen time — particularly passive viewing — is associated with risks including depression, sleep problems, and social-emotional difficulties, especially in young children. Up to roughly two hours per day may not be associated with depression in children aged 5-18, and content type meaningfully shapes outcomes.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The word 'destroying' implies universal, severe, and direct causation across all children and all screen use. The actual evidence shows associations (not established causation), meaningful variation by dose and content type, often small effect sizes, and high heterogeneity across studies. The blanket framing erases the dose-response and content distinctions the evidence supports.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: High volumes of passive screen use are consistently associated with worse outcomes across multiple domains for children, particularly the very young.

the_noise.claim: Tiger parenting produces superior child outcomes.
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Tiger parenting may be associated with certain academic pressures, but the empirical evidence finds supportive parenting (high warmth plus structure) linked to better overall developmental outcomes and GPA, while tiger parenting is linked to higher depressive symptoms and anxiety.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: 'Superior outcomes' implies advantage across the board. The research shows trade-offs: any academic associations come alongside documented mental health costs. The construct also does not appear to be as prevalent in practice as popular accounts suggest.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: High parental involvement and structure are associated with positive educational outcomes — but those components appear to work better when combined with warmth rather than pressure.

still_worth_verifying.question: Does free-range parenting directly produce better outcomes, or does the evidence only establish that overprotective parenting produces worse ones?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: The visitor's claim pairs these as opposites, but the research packet shows evidence runs mostly in one direction — harms of overprotection — while direct evidence for free-range parenting outcomes is limited. The policy and practical implications differ depending on which is true.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Studies with standardized definitions of free-range parenting measuring child outcomes directly, rather than inferring them from overprotective parenting research. Research accounting for neighborhood safety and socioeconomic context would also sharpen the picture.

still_worth_verifying.question: What is the causal direction between screen time and child depression or social-emotional difficulties?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: If children with emerging mental health difficulties gravitate toward more screen use, reducing screens may not address the underlying problem. The direction of causation shapes whether screen-time limits are an effective intervention.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Experimental or quasi-experimental studies with random assignment to screen-time conditions, or stronger longitudinal designs that control for pre-existing mental health status.

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Whether a specific child's screen habits — given their age, content, social context, and existing wellbeing — are at a harmful level.
Whether a particular family's parenting approach lands closer to 'supportive structure' or 'tiger parenting' in the sense the research measures.
Whether homework at a specific grade level and in specific quantities is helping or hurting a particular child's learning or wellbeing.

supported_takeaways: For screen time, how much and what type both matter: the evidence for harm is stronger for high volumes of passive viewing, weaker or absent for moderate educational and interactive use. 'All screens are harmful' is not what the research supports.

Tiger parenting is not supported as a superior overall strategy: longitudinal evidence links it to worse mental health outcomes, while supportive parenting (warm and structured) is associated with better results across domains.

Homework appears to have a real but age-dependent relationship with achievement — meaningful for older students, weak to negligible for younger ones, and potentially counterproductive when excessive or when heavy parental involvement substitutes for the child's own effort.
treat_skeptically: Any claim that screen time universally 'destroys' children — the evidence is about dose, content, and age, not a blanket harm.
The popular tiger parenting narrative that strict, high-pressure parenting produces children who outperform — the empirical record shows this framing misses significant mental health costs.

The implied binary between tiger parenting and free-range parenting — the research identifies supportive parenting (warm plus structured) as a distinct and better-supported approach, not simply a midpoint.
what_would_change_the_answer: Experimental evidence establishing whether screen time reductions causally improve child outcomes, or whether the association runs the other way.
Standardized definitions and direct outcome studies for free-range parenting that go beyond inferring benefits from the harms of overprotection.
Cross-cultural replication of tiger parenting research beyond Asian and Asian-American samples, to clarify how much cultural context shapes the findings.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Research showing an association between a factor and an outcome under specific conditions — age group, content type, dose level — gets restated as a universal claim applying to all children in all circumstances. The conditions drop out in popular retelling.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Look for absolute language ('destroys,' 'always,' 'superior') where the underlying study measured averages, associations, or outcomes in a defined subgroup. If no age range, content type, or dosage is mentioned alongside the claim, the original conditions have likely been stripped away.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Most studies in this area measure associations between parenting behaviors and child outcomes without being able to establish which caused which. Claims that a parenting approach 'produces' a result go beyond what the observational data supports.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Check whether the research design involved random assignment or strong controls for pre-existing differences. If not, phrases like 'leads to,' 'causes,' or 'produces' in summaries of the research are doing more than the data can support.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A parenting style or practice may show a benefit on one measured outcome (e.g., academic scores) while showing costs on another (e.g., anxiety, emotional wellbeing). Advocates selectively highlight the favorable outcome and omit the trade-offs.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: When a claim cites only academic or only mental health outcomes, ask whether the same research measured outcomes in the other domain — and whether those results were mentioned.

input.topic: Everyone needs exactly 8 hours of sleep or their health suffers
input.conflictingAdvice: My coworker says blue light glasses fixed her insomnia. Another friend says sleep debt cannot be repaid on weekends, but my doctor said catching up on weekends helps.

output.topic_as_understood: Three related sleep claims: whether everyone needs exactly 8 hours, whether blue light glasses reliably fix insomnia, and whether weekend sleep can or cannot repay sleep debt.
output.framing: Each claim collapses a range into an absolute. The evidence consistently shows gradients and conditions where the popular version says a bright line.

items.claim: Most adults need somewhere in the range of 7–9 hours, not exactly 8, and the right amount varies by person and age.
items.basis: The National Sleep Foundation reviewed over 130 meta-analyses and set a recommended range of 7–9 hours for adults — not a fixed 8. Major bodies including the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommend at least 7 hours. A large population study found that both very short and very long sleep were associated with worse health outcomes, with the healthier pattern centered around 6–8 hours.
items.limits: Recommended ranges come from epidemiological associations, not controlled trials proving causation for every health outcome. Self-reported sleep times, which most studies rely on, may not reflect actual sleep. A small number of people may genuinely function well outside the 7–9 hour range.

items.claim: Weekend catch-up sleep offers partial, real benefit over staying chronically deprived, but does not fully undo the damage from regular short sleep.
items.basis: A 2025 systematic review found catch-up sleep can improve mood, reduce fatigue, and restore some cognitive performance short-term, but is not a sustainable repayment strategy. One study found that after a week of restricted sleep, two nights of recovery sleep did not fully restore attention or insulin sensitivity. A longer-term study found people who caught up on weekends had better survival outcomes than those who remained deprived all week, suggesting real but limited benefit.
items.limits: The survival study is observational and cannot establish causation. How much catch-up helps likely depends on how severe and prolonged the deficit is. Sleeping in significantly can also shift the circadian clock, creating 'social jet lag' associated with its own metabolic costs.

the_noise.claim: Everyone needs exactly 8 hours of sleep or their health suffers.
the_noise.noise_label: Collapsing a range into a single number
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Most adults function best somewhere within a 7–9 hour range, with individual variation, and sleep quality and regularity matter alongside duration.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The claim fixes one number where the evidence supports a range, and treats duration as the only variable when professional guidance treats it as one component among several.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Getting close to 8 hours puts most adults near the middle of the recommended range, so the number is not arbitrary — it just does not apply identically to everyone.

the_noise.claim: Blue light glasses fixed insomnia (implying they reliably improve sleep for people with insomnia).
the_noise.noise_label: One person's result generalized to a reliable fix
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Blue-light blocking glasses show promise for some clinical populations, but trial results are split roughly evenly between showing benefit and showing no significant effect — and the quality and filtering specification of the glasses matter considerably.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: A single person's reported improvement is being treated as evidence that the intervention works reliably. The research base is inconsistent: one Cochrane-indexed review found three RCTs showing benefit and three showing none. There is also a documented gap between subjective improvement and objective sleep measures.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: There is a plausible biological rationale and some positive trial evidence, particularly for people with insomnia, delayed sleep phase, or shift work — the coworker's experience is not implausible, but it cannot be assumed to generalize.

the_noise.claim: Sleep debt cannot be repaid on weekends at all (friend's absolute version).
the_noise.noise_label: Treating partial recovery as no recovery
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Full repayment of chronic sleep debt over a weekend is not supported, but partial recovery — improved mood, reduced fatigue, some cognitive restoration, and possibly better long-term health outcomes compared to sustained deprivation — is documented.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The friend's claim is correct that a weekend cannot erase a chronic deficit, but it overstates the case by implying catch-up sleep provides no benefit, when the evidence shows meaningful partial benefit over not recovering at all.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Weekend sleep is not a reliable substitute for consistent adequate nightly sleep, and relying on it as a strategy carries real costs including social jet lag.

still_worth_verifying.question: Do blue-light blocking glasses help people without diagnosed sleep disorders, or is the benefit mainly in clinical populations?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Most of the positive evidence comes from people with insomnia, delayed sleep phase, or shift work. Whether healthy adults with ordinary screen exposure benefit is less established, which affects whether the coworker's experience is likely to transfer to others.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Larger RCTs in non-clinical populations using glasses that meet a specified melanopic filtering threshold, with both subjective and objective sleep outcome measures.

still_worth_verifying.question: How much does the severity and duration of sleep debt affect how much weekend catch-up sleep can restore?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: The doctor and friend may both be right in different circumstances — mild short-term debt may be more recoverable than months of chronic restriction. The right advice likely depends on which situation applies.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Studies that vary the depth and length of accumulated deficit and track multiple recovery markers, including metabolic and cognitive outcomes, over longer follow-up periods.

what_general_claims_cant_decide: How many hours this particular person actually needs, which can only be determined by tracking their own sleep, daytime functioning, and energy across consistent conditions.
Whether the coworker's insomnia improvement from blue-light glasses reflects a genuine circadian effect, a placebo response, or some other change she made at the same time.
Whether the doctor's advice about catching up on weekends was tailored to the visitor's specific pattern of sleep loss, which would change whether it applies.

supported_takeaways: For most adults, anywhere from 7 to 9 hours is the evidence-supported target range — 8 is a reasonable midpoint, not a universal requirement.
Weekend catch-up sleep is genuinely better than staying deprived, but it does not fully restore what chronic short sleep costs, and relying on it habitually carries its own risks.
Blue-light glasses have mixed trial evidence — plausible and possibly helpful, especially for people with diagnosed sleep problems, but not a proven fix even for insomnia.
treat_skeptically: Any claim that a single number applies to every adult's sleep need.
Treating one person's positive experience with blue-light glasses as evidence the product reliably works for others.
The absolute version of 'you cannot repay sleep debt at all' — partial recovery is real, even if full recovery is not.
what_would_change_the_answer: Larger, well-controlled RCTs on blue-light glasses in non-clinical populations would clarify whether the benefit extends beyond people with diagnosed sleep disorders.

Studies tracking cognitive, metabolic, and health outcomes of habitual weekend catch-up sleep over months or years would better establish whether it is a viable long-term strategy or a consistently poor one.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A recommended range like 7–9 hours gets simplified to one memorable number — 8 — which then gets treated as a universal requirement rather than a population midpoint.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: The claim states one figure with no acknowledgment of variation; professional guidance documents typically list a range rather than a single number.

sources_of_noise.source_type: Personal anecdote generalized to reliable effect
sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: One person's improvement with a product or intervention gets communicated as evidence the intervention works, when it could reflect genuine effect, placebo, or coincidence — and the underlying trial evidence may be split.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: The claim starts with 'it worked for my [friend/coworker]' and implies it will therefore work, without reference to what controlled studies found.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A finding that full recovery is not achieved gets repackaged as 'no recovery is possible,' erasing the meaningful partial benefit the evidence does support.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: The claim uses words like 'cannot,' 'never,' or 'impossible' in a domain where the evidence shows differences in degree rather than a binary outcome.
